reasons.name: Late loading
reasons.meaning: The vehicle was ready, the load was not. Loading started late, ran slow or waited for missing parcels.
moves: Give every route a fixed loading start time and a loading slot at a named dock.
Stage the load by route before the vehicle arrives, so loading is carrying, not searching.
Time loading for one week: find the routes that always take longer and why.
reasons.question: What is the vehicle waiting for in the last fifteen minutes before it leaves?

reasons.name: Late wave or volume peak
reasons.meaning: Volume arrived after the cut-off, or a peak landed on the same departure slots every day. The routes wait for the last parcels.
moves: Agree a hard cut-off: parcels that miss it go on the next route, not into a late departure.
Move the heaviest routes away from the peak wave where the delivery windows allow it.
Share late-wave numbers with the upstream site or sorter every day, with the departures they cost.
reasons.question: Who decides to hold a route for late volume, and what does it cost the first customers?

reasons.name: Vehicle not ready
reasons.meaning: The vehicle arrived late at the dock, failed a check or was not fuelled or charged.
moves: Check, fuel or charge vehicles at the end of the previous shift, not at departure.
Keep one spare vehicle ready at peak, with keys and paperwork.
Log vehicle problems by plate: a few vehicles usually cause most of it.
reasons.question: When do we find out a vehicle is not ready, and could we know an hour earlier?

reasons.name: Driver not ready
reasons.meaning: The driver arrived late, the briefing ran long or the route was reassigned at the last minute.
moves: Start the briefing on time and keep it short; hand route notes over in writing.
Confirm drivers for early routes the evening before.
Keep reassignments before loading starts, never at the vehicle.
reasons.question: How many minutes pass between the driver arriving and the vehicle leaving, and where do they go?

reasons.name: Missing paperwork or scanner
reasons.meaning: Scanners, keys, delivery notes or customs papers were not ready when the vehicle was.
moves: Prepare scanners, keys and papers per route in one place before loading ends.
Charge and test scanners at the end of each shift.
Add papers and devices to the departure check, not to the driver's memory.
reasons.question: What does a driver have to go and find before leaving?

reasons.name: Traffic or roadworks
reasons.meaning: The route lost time to traffic, closures or roadworks. Some of it is outside your control; recurring patterns are not.
moves: Look for the same roads and hours in the log: recurring traffic belongs in the route plan.
Shift departures or stop order to miss known peaks.
Check whether the planned time includes realistic driving time for that hour.
reasons.question: Is this traffic a surprise, or does it happen at this hour every week?

reasons.name: Address or access
reasons.meaning: Wrong addresses, closed gates, no parking or unclear delivery points cost minutes at each stop.
moves: Collect access notes (gates, codes, loading zones) and put them in the route data.
Fix wrong addresses at the source, not by memory of one driver.
Give new drivers the notes for difficult stops before they leave.
reasons.question: Which stops cost more than ten minutes every time, and does the next driver know?

reasons.name: Customer not available
reasons.meaning: The customer was not there, so the driver waited, called or came back.
moves: Send a delivery window to the customer and confirm it before the route leaves.
Agree a fixed waiting time and a clear next step for each type of customer.
Look for repeat customers: a standing delivery arrangement saves the same minutes every week.
reasons.question: How long does a driver wait before moving on, and who decided that?

reasons.name: Too many stops
reasons.meaning: The route was planned with more stops or distance than the time allows. The driver cannot win it back.
moves: Compare planned and actual stop times per route: plan with what really happens.
Cap stops per route by area and time of day, not by average.
Move stops from the longest routes before the vehicle is loaded.
reasons.question: Could our best driver finish this route on time on a normal day?

reasons.name: Weather
reasons.meaning: Snow, storms or heat slowed driving and stops.
moves: Plan weather days: fewer stops per route and earlier departures when a warning is out.
Tell customers early when windows will move.
Keep weather out of the other reasons, so the normal pattern stays visible.
reasons.question: What do we change in the plan the evening before bad weather?

dock.name: Dock
dock.lede: started at the dock, before the vehicle left
dock.advice: Fix the departure first. A vehicle that leaves 30 minutes late cannot be on time for its first stops, whatever the driver does on the road.

road.name: Road
road.lede: were built on the road, after an on-time departure
road.advice: The dock hands over on time; the delay grows on the road. Look at route design, stop count and delivery windows before you look at driving.

checklist: Loading starts at a fixed time for every route, not when the last parcel arrives.
The cut-off holds: late volume goes to the next route, not into a late departure.
Vehicles are checked, fuelled or charged and at the dock before loading starts.
Drivers are briefed and ready before their vehicle is loaded.
Routes with the earliest delivery windows load and leave first.
Scanners, keys and paperwork are ready per route before loading ends.
Departure times are recorded for every route, not only the late ones.
Routes are planned with a realistic number of stops for the time available.
Known access problems (gates, codes, loading zones) are in the route notes.
Every late route has a reason recorded the same day.
